tools.name: configuration_view

tools.name: events_list
tools.description: List Kubernetes events (warnings, errors, state changes) for debugging and troubleshooting in the current cluster from all namespaces

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter events by field values (e.g. 'type=Warning', 'involvedObject.name=my-pod'). Supported fields: involvedObject.kind, involvedObject.name, involvedObject.namespace, involvedObject.uid, involvedObject.apiVersion, involvedObject.resourceVersion, involvedObject.fieldPath, reason, reportingComponent, source, type. namespace.description: Optional Namespace to retrieve the events from. If not provided, will list events from all namespaces

tools.name: namespaces_list
tools.description: List all the Kubernetes namespaces in the current cluster

fieldSelector.description: Optional Kubernetes field selector to filter namespaces by field values (e.g. 'metadata.name=default', 'status.phase=Active'). Supported fields: metadata.name, status.phase. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/field-selectors/

tools.name: nodes_log
tools.description: Get logs from a Kubernetes node (kubelet, kube-proxy, or other system logs). This accesses node logs through the Kubernetes API proxy to the kubelet

name.description: Name of the node to get logs from

query.description: query specifies services(s) or files from which to return logs (required). Example: "kubelet" to fetch kubelet logs, "/<log-file-name>" to fetch a specific log file from the node (e.g., "/var/log/kubelet.log" or "/var/log/kube-proxy.log")

tailLines.description: Number of lines to retrieve from the end of the logs (Optional, 0 means all logs)

tools.name: nodes_stats_summary
tools.description: Get detailed resource usage statistics from a Kubernetes node via the kubelet's Summary API. Provides comprehensive metrics including CPU, memory, filesystem, and network usage at the node, pod, and container levels. On systems with cgroup v2 and kernel 4.20+, also includes PSI (Pressure Stall Information) metrics that show resource pressure for CPU, memory, and I/O. See https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/instrumentation/understand-psi-metrics/ for details on PSI metrics

name.description: Name of the node to get stats from

Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine with containerPort: 80
  - Security config: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed version selector) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1.

Resulting traffic split
- With 2 replicas in engine-v2-0 and 2 in engine-v2-1, the ClusterIP Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across the 4 pods.

Verification
- Pods running:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 Ready
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Ready
- Service selector: app=recommendation-engine
- Note: The Service targetPort is 8080 (unchanged from stable). The stable Deployment advertises containerPort 80, which we matched. This is fine if the container actually listens on 8080 (typical for nginx-unprivileged). If your container listens on 80 instead, let me know and I can switch the Service targetPort to 80.

Roll back or adjust
- To stop canary traffic: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To remove the canary: delete Deployment engine-v2-1.

Steps.message:
namespace/canary-deployment-ns created
deployment.apps/engine-v2-0 created
service/recommendation-engine created

Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine with containerPort: 80
  - Security config: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed version selector) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1.

Resulting traffic split
- With 2 replicas in engine-v2-0 and 2 in engine-v2-1, the ClusterIP Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across the 4 pods.

Verification
- Pods running:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 Ready
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Ready
- Service selector: app=recommendation-engine
- Note: The Service targetPort is 8080 (unchanged from stable). The stable Deployment advertises containerPort 80, which we matched. This is fine if the container actually listens on 8080 (typical for nginx-unprivileged). If your container listens on 80 instead, let me know and I can switch the Service targetPort to 80.

Roll back or adjust
- To stop canary traffic: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To remove the canary: delete Deployment engine-v2-1.

Done. Here’s what I set up and verified:

What I deployed
- Canary Deployment: engine-v2-1 (namespace: canary-deployment-ns)
  - Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.29
  - Replicas: 2
  - Labels: app=recommendation-engine, version=v2.1
  - Container: rec-engine with containerPort: 80
  - Security config: same as stable (no explicit securityContext)
- Service update: recommendation-engine now selects app=recommendation-engine (removed version selector) so it targets both engine-v2-0 and engine-v2-1.

Resulting traffic split
- With 2 replicas in engine-v2-0 and 2 in engine-v2-1, the ClusterIP Service will distribute roughly 50/50 across the 4 pods.

Verification
- Pods running:
  - engine-v2-0: 2/2 Ready
  - engine-v2-1: 2/2 Ready
- Service selector: app=recommendation-engine
- Note: The Service targetPort is 8080 (unchanged from stable). The stable Deployment advertises containerPort 80, which we matched. This is fine if the container actually listens on 8080 (typical for nginx-unprivileged). If your container listens on 80 instead, let me know and I can switch the Service targetPort to 80.

Roll back or adjust
- To stop canary traffic: set the Service selector back to app=recommendation-engine,version=v2.0.
- To remove the canary: delete Deployment engine-v2-1.

outputSteps.content:
Done.

What I found
- Root cause: The Deployment overrode the container entrypoint with /bin/sh -c nonexistent_command, causing the pod to exit immediately. Pod logs: “/bin/sh: 1: nonexistent_command: not found”.

What I changed
- Recreated the app Deployment without the custom command/args so the image’s default NGINX entrypoint runs.
- Image: quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged
- Exposed containerPort 8080
- imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent

Verification
- New pod: app-c88f5d4bc-nc942
- Status: 1/1 Running, 0 restarts, namespace: crashloop-test

Note
- I deleted and recreated the Deployment to fully remove the bad command/args, which caused brief downtime. If you prefer an in-place update next time to avoid deletion, I can patch it instead.

results.taskOutput:
I found the issue: the Deployment was using an invalid image tag (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag), causing ImagePullBackOff.

What I changed:
- Updated the container image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
- Set imagePullPolicy to Always so the new image is pulled immediately

Current status:
- Deployment debug/app is Available (1/1)
- Pod app-6d98fd7d7f-m2wlb is Running and Ready

Notes:
- Previous warning events show ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff due to the invalid tag.
- If you prefer reproducible deployments, I can pin to a specific version tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.27.x).

outputSteps.content:
I found the issue: the Deployment was using an invalid image tag (quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:invalid-tag), causing ImagePullBackOff.

What I changed:
- Updated the container image to quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:latest
- Set imagePullPolicy to Always so the new image is pulled immediately

Current status:
- Deployment debug/app is Available (1/1)
- Pod app-6d98fd7d7f-m2wlb is Running and Ready

Notes:
- Previous warning events show ErrImagePull/ImagePullBackOff due to the invalid tag.
- If you prefer reproducible deployments, I can pin to a specific version tag (e.g., quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged:1.27.x).

results.taskOutput:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind and the scheduler blocked the pod.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it with the working StorageClass "standard" (minikube hostpath), size 1Gi, ReadWriteOnce.

Current status
- Pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns: Running and Ready.
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to a PV.

Notes
- No data loss: the original PVC never bound to a volume.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), tell me and I can switch it.

Steps.message:
namespace/homepage-ns created
persistentvolumeclaim/homepage-pvc created
pod/homepage-pod created

I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind and the scheduler blocked the pod.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it with the working StorageClass "standard" (minikube hostpath), size 1Gi, ReadWriteOnce.

Current status
- Pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns: Running and Ready.
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to a PV.

Notes
- No data loss: the original PVC never bound to a volume.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), tell me and I can switch it.

outputSteps.content:
I fixed it.

What was wrong
- The pod was Pending because its PVC (homepage-pvc) referenced a non-existent StorageClass "sc", so the claim couldn’t bind and the scheduler blocked the pod.

What I changed
- Deleted the unbound PVC homepage-pvc.
- Recreated it with the working StorageClass "standard" (minikube hostpath), size 1Gi, ReadWriteOnce.

Current status
- Pod homepage-pod in homepage-ns: Running and Ready.
- PVC homepage-pvc: Bound (1Gi) to a PV.

Notes
- No data loss: the original PVC never bound to a volume.
- If you prefer a different StorageClass (e.g., csi-hostpath-sc), tell me and I can switch it.

results.taskOutput:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root), but the Deployment probes and Service were using port 80.
- This caused liveness/readiness probe failures and the Service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to expose container port 8080 and changed both liveness and readiness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to keep service port 80 but targetPort 8080 (so clients use port 80, which forwards to 8080 in the pod).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-5d86754686-9l7mv).
- Service: orders/webapp is healthy and has a ready endpoint. Service port 80 maps to container port 8080.

How to test
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080/
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/

If you need external access, there’s no Ingress/Route defined yet. Tell me the hostname/path you want, and I can create it.

Steps.message:
namespace/orders created
deployment.apps/webapp created
service/webapp created
Waiting for pod to start and begin failing health checks...
deployment.apps/webapp condition met
Setup successful: Deployment is no longer available.

I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root), but the Deployment probes and Service were using port 80.
- This caused liveness/readiness probe failures and the Service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to expose container port 8080 and changed both liveness and readiness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to keep service port 80 but targetPort 8080 (so clients use port 80, which forwards to 8080 in the pod).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-5d86754686-9l7mv).
- Service: orders/webapp is healthy and has a ready endpoint. Service port 80 maps to container port 8080.

How to test
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080/
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/

If you need external access, there’s no Ingress/Route defined yet. Tell me the hostname/path you want, and I can create it.

outputSteps.content:
I found and fixed the issue.

What was wrong
- The image quay.io/nginx/nginx-unprivileged listens on port 8080 (non-root), but the Deployment probes and Service were using port 80.
- This caused liveness/readiness probe failures and the Service had no ready endpoints.

What I changed
- Updated the Deployment to expose container port 8080 and changed both liveness and readiness probes to HTTP GET / on port 8080.
- Updated the Service to keep service port 80 but targetPort 8080 (so clients use port 80, which forwards to 8080 in the pod).

Current status
- Pod: 1/1 Running and Ready (orders/webapp-5d86754686-9l7mv).
- Service: orders/webapp is healthy and has a ready endpoint. Service port 80 maps to container port 8080.

How to test
- From your machine: kubectl -n orders port-forward svc/webapp 8080:80 and browse http://localhost:8080/
- In-cluster: curl http://webapp.orders.svc.cluster.local/

If you need external access, there’s no Ingress/Route defined yet. Tell me the hostname/path you want, and I can create it.

results.taskOutput:
Fixed.

What was wrong:
- The Role bound to serviceaccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the SA couldn’t list pods.

What I changed:
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - verbs: get, list, watch
  - resources: pods
- Kept the existing deployments list permission.
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the pod-reader SA, so no change was needed there.

How to verify:
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- Or try listing: kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

If you still can’t list pods, ensure your command targets the simple-rbac-setup namespace and that you’re impersonating/using the pod-reader service account.

Steps.message:
namespace/simple-rbac-setup created
serviceaccount/pod-reader created
role.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-role created
rolebinding.rbac.authorization.k8s.io/pod-reader-binding created

Fixed.

What was wrong:
- The Role bound to serviceaccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the SA couldn’t list pods.

What I changed:
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - verbs: get, list, watch
  - resources: pods
- Kept the existing deployments list permission.
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the pod-reader SA, so no change was needed there.

How to verify:
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- Or try listing: kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

If you still can’t list pods, ensure your command targets the simple-rbac-setup namespace and that you’re impersonating/using the pod-reader service account.

outputSteps.content:
Fixed.

What was wrong:
- The Role bound to serviceaccount simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader only allowed listing apps/deployments, not core/v1 pods. So the SA couldn’t list pods.

What I changed:
- Updated Role simple-rbac-setup/pod-reader-role to include permissions on core/v1 pods:
  - verbs: get, list, watch
  - resources: pods
- Kept the existing deployments list permission.
- The existing RoleBinding pod-reader-binding already targets this Role and the pod-reader SA, so no change was needed there.

How to verify:
- kubectl auth can-i --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup list pods
- Or try listing: kubectl --as=system:serviceaccount:simple-rbac-setup:pod-reader -n simple-rbac-setup get pods

If you still can’t list pods, ensure your command targets the simple-rbac-setup namespace and that you’re impersonating/using the pod-reader service account.

Steps.message: Verification successful: RBAC role correctly reconfigured.

results.taskOutput:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pod label is app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no Endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the Pod.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Result: even if the selector matched, traffic would have been sent to the wrong port.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service web/nginx to:
  - selector: app=nginx (matches the Deployment)
  - targetPort: 8080 (matches container’s listen port)
  - Preserved the existing ClusterIP
- Outcome: Endpoints are now populated and point to the Pod at port 8080.

Current state (post-fix)
- Service: ClusterIP 10.96.105.148, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.26:8080 (nginx-6d94b64d45-jnkm2)
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster (e.g., http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local on port 80).

How to verify (you can run any of these)
- From another Pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl run -n web curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -it --rm -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://nginx'
- Or port-forward from your workstation:
  - kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
  - Then visit http://localhost:8080

Note on external access
- The Service type is ClusterIP (internal-only). If you need external access, I can:
  - Switch to NodePort (easiest): expose on a node port, e.g., 30080
  - Create an Ingress (preferred in many setups) or a LoadBalancer Service (if your cluster supports it)
- Tell me which exposure method you prefer and I’ll configure it.

Steps.message:
namespace/web created
deployment.apps/nginx created
service/nginx created

Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pod label is app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no Endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the Pod.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Result: even if the selector matched, traffic would have been sent to the wrong port.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service web/nginx to:
  - selector: app=nginx (matches the Deployment)
  - targetPort: 8080 (matches container’s listen port)
  - Preserved the existing ClusterIP
- Outcome: Endpoints are now populated and point to the Pod at port 8080.

Current state (post-fix)
- Service: ClusterIP 10.96.105.148, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.26:8080 (nginx-6d94b64d45-jnkm2)
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster (e.g., http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local on port 80).

How to verify (you can run any of these)
- From another Pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl run -n web curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -it --rm -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://nginx'
- Or port-forward from your workstation:
  - kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
  - Then visit http://localhost:8080

Note on external access
- The Service type is ClusterIP (internal-only). If you need external access, I can:
  - Switch to NodePort (easiest): expose on a node port, e.g., 30080
  - Create an Ingress (preferred in many setups) or a LoadBalancer Service (if your cluster supports it)
- Tell me which exposure method you prefer and I’ll configure it.

outputSteps.content:
Diagnosis
- The Service selector didn’t match the Pod labels:
  - Service selector was app=web
  - Deployment/Pod label is app=nginx
  - Result: the Service had no Endpoints, so traffic couldn’t reach the Pod.
- The nginx-unprivileged image listens on port 8080, but the Service targetPort was 80.
  - Result: even if the selector matched, traffic would have been sent to the wrong port.

What I changed (fix applied)
- Updated Service web/nginx to:
  - selector: app=nginx (matches the Deployment)
  - targetPort: 8080 (matches container’s listen port)
  - Preserved the existing ClusterIP
- Outcome: Endpoints are now populated and point to the Pod at port 8080.

Current state (post-fix)
- Service: ClusterIP 10.96.105.148, port 80 -> targetPort 8080, selector app=nginx
- Endpoints: 10.244.0.26:8080 (nginx-6d94b64d45-jnkm2)
- The nginx Service is now reachable inside the cluster (e.g., http://nginx.web.svc.cluster.local on port 80).

How to verify (you can run any of these)
- From another Pod in the cluster:
  - kubectl run -n web curl --image=curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -it --rm -- sh -lc 'curl -sI http://nginx'
- Or port-forward from your workstation:
  - kubectl -n web port-forward svc/nginx 8080:80
  - Then visit http://localhost:8080

Note on external access
- The Service type is ClusterIP (internal-only). If you need external access, I can:
  - Switch to NodePort (easiest): expose on a node port, e.g., 30080
  - Create an Ingress (preferred in many setups) or a LoadBalancer Service (if your cluster supports it)
- Tell me which exposure method you prefer and I’ll configure it.

results.taskOutput:
Summary of what I found and fixed
- Root cause: Your backend Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster’s single node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler therefore couldn’t place any pods:
  - Events: FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Result: web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local failed.
- Fix applied:
  - Removed the restrictive nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it.
  - Deployment now has 2 replicas running: web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-46882 and -ptrt6.
  - Service endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80 for web-app-service.

Details
- Before:
  - Pods: Pending (0/1) due to nodeSelector mismatch.
  - Service: ClusterIP present, but Endpoints: <none>.
- After:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running on node mcp-eval-cluster.
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80 for web-app-service in webshop-frontend.

What you can do to verify from your side
- From your workstation:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
  - Optional in-cluster test:
    - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 -- sh
    - Inside the shell: curl -I http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/

Notes and recommendations
- If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you actually want these pods on special GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the intended nodes with environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations to match real node labels/taints.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the Deployment so the Service only sends traffic once the container is ready, for example:
  - HTTP GET / on port 80 with initialDelaySeconds and periodSeconds tuned for your app.

If you want, I can reintroduce a corrected nodeSelector (or label your nodes) based on your intended scheduling policy.

namespace/webshop-frontend created
service/web-app-service created
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment created
Waiting for resources to be created...
deployment.apps/web-app-deployment condition met
Warning: v1 Endpoints is deprecated in v1.33+; use discovery.k8s.io/v1 EndpointSlice
Setup successful: Service has no endpoints as expected

Summary of what I found and fixed
- Root cause: Your backend Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster’s single node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler therefore couldn’t place any pods:
  - Events: FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Result: web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local failed.
- Fix applied:
  - Removed the restrictive nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it.
  - Deployment now has 2 replicas running: web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-46882 and -ptrt6.
  - Service endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80 for web-app-service.

Details
- Before:
  - Pods: Pending (0/1) due to nodeSelector mismatch.
  - Service: ClusterIP present, but Endpoints: <none>.
- After:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running on node mcp-eval-cluster.
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80 for web-app-service in webshop-frontend.

What you can do to verify from your side
- From your workstation:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
  - Optional in-cluster test:
    - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 -- sh
    - Inside the shell: curl -I http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/

Notes and recommendations
- If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you actually want these pods on special GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the intended nodes with environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations to match real node labels/taints.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the Deployment so the Service only sends traffic once the container is ready, for example:
  - HTTP GET / on port 80 with initialDelaySeconds and periodSeconds tuned for your app.

If you want, I can reintroduce a corrected nodeSelector (or label your nodes) based on your intended scheduling policy.

outputSteps.content:
Summary of what I found and fixed
- Root cause: Your backend Deployment (web-app-deployment) had a nodeSelector: environment=production-gpu, but the cluster’s single node doesn’t have that label. The scheduler therefore couldn’t place any pods:
  - Events: FailedScheduling: “0/1 nodes are available: 1 node(s) didn’t match Pod’s node affinity/selector.”
  - Result: web-app-service had no endpoints, so connections to web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local failed.
- Fix applied:
  - Removed the restrictive nodeSelector by recreating the Deployment without it.
  - Deployment now has 2 replicas running: web-app-deployment-6748d646cb-46882 and -ptrt6.
  - Service endpoints are now populated: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80 for web-app-service.

Details
- Before:
  - Pods: Pending (0/1) due to nodeSelector mismatch.
  - Service: ClusterIP present, but Endpoints: <none>.
- After:
  - Pods: 2/2 Running on node mcp-eval-cluster.
  - Endpoints: 10.244.0.30:80, 10.244.0.31:80 for web-app-service in webshop-frontend.

What you can do to verify from your side
- From your workstation:
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get pods -o wide
  - kubectl -n webshop-frontend get endpoints web-app-service
  - Optional in-cluster test:
    - kubectl -n webshop-frontend run curl --rm -it --image=curlimages/curl:8.8.0 -- sh
    - Inside the shell: curl -I http://web-app-service.webshop-frontend.svc.cluster.local/

Notes and recommendations
- If the nodeSelector was intentional (e.g., you actually want these pods on special GPU nodes), either:
  - Label the intended nodes with environment=production-gpu, or
  - Adjust the Deployment’s nodeSelector/tolerations to match real node labels/taints.
- Consider adding a readinessProbe to the Deployment so the Service only sends traffic once the container is ready, for example:
  - HTTP GET / on port 80 with initialDelaySeconds and periodSeconds tuned for your app.

If you want, I can reintroduce a corrected nodeSelector (or label your nodes) based on your intended scheduling policy.

- Restarted the storage-pod to complete the filesystem resize on the node.

- storage-pod has been recreated and is starting with the resized volume.

Optional verification
- Inside the pod, check disk size at /usr/share/nginx/html with df -h to confirm the filesystem reflects 3Gi.

results.taskOutput:
All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC, service accounts, resource quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege, multi-tenant dev environment for Alice, Bob, and Charlie.

What was created

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod
- Labels added for policy scoping (e.g., env: dev|staging|prod)

2) RBAC and Service Accounts
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to own namespace (least-privilege):
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding ClusterRole edit to:
    - the user (alice|bob|charlie)
    - the service account (alice-sa|bob-sa|charlie-sa)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - users: alice, bob, charlie
    - service accounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No developer bindings were created in staging or prod (only cluster admins will have access by virtue of their cluster-admin privileges)

Notes on least privilege:
- edit grants full CRUD on namespaced resources but not RBAC; this keeps developers from altering RBAC while letting them manage everything else in their own namespace
- view is read-only and does not include secrets by default (safer for dev-shared). If you need read access to secrets there, tell me and I’ll add a narrowly scoped Role.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi
  - requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi
  - requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-* / dev-shared / staging / prod)
- DNS/system egress:
  - Allow egress on TCP/UDP 53 to kube-system (CoreDNS) in all created namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - Ingress: allow only from same namespace and from dev-shared
  - Egress: allow only to same namespace and to dev-shared
  - This blocks cross-developer communication and limits access to dev-shared only
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress: allow from namespaces labeled env=dev (the three dev namespaces and dev-shared itself)
  - Egress: allow to namespaces labeled env=dev
- staging and prod:
  - Strictly isolated from dev namespaces
  - Ingress: allow only from same namespace
  - Egress: allow only to same namespace
  - Plus DNS egress as above

Operational notes
- A NetworkPolicy-capable CNI (e.g., Calico, Cilium) must be active for these policies to take effect.
- RBAC is additive. Since we did not grant developers any roles in staging/prod, they cannot access those namespaces unless they already have cluster-wide roles (cluster-admins will continue to have access).
- view in dev-shared does not include reading Secrets by default. If developers must read specific Secrets, I can add a tightly scoped Role to allow get on specific secrets only.

Quick verification tips
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC access checks (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice     → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i delete deploy -n dev-shared --as alice → no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice        → no
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota compute-and-services-quota
- NetworkPolicies: kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy

If you want me to:
- Bind a specific “cluster-admins” group explicitly in staging/prod for clarity
- Allow read of specific Secrets in dev-shared
- Add LimitRanges (default requests/limits per pod/container)
…say the word and I’ll apply those too.

Steps.message:
Setting up cluster state for dev environment eval...
Setup completed successfully

All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC, service accounts, resource quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege, multi-tenant dev environment for Alice, Bob, and Charlie.

What was created

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod
- Labels added for policy scoping (e.g., env: dev|staging|prod)

2) RBAC and Service Accounts
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to own namespace (least-privilege):
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding ClusterRole edit to:
    - the user (alice|bob|charlie)
    - the service account (alice-sa|bob-sa|charlie-sa)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - users: alice, bob, charlie
    - service accounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No developer bindings were created in staging or prod (only cluster admins will have access by virtue of their cluster-admin privileges)

Notes on least privilege:
- edit grants full CRUD on namespaced resources but not RBAC; this keeps developers from altering RBAC while letting them manage everything else in their own namespace
- view is read-only and does not include secrets by default (safer for dev-shared). If you need read access to secrets there, tell me and I’ll add a narrowly scoped Role.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi
  - requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi
  - requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-* / dev-shared / staging / prod)
- DNS/system egress:
  - Allow egress on TCP/UDP 53 to kube-system (CoreDNS) in all created namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - Ingress: allow only from same namespace and from dev-shared
  - Egress: allow only to same namespace and to dev-shared
  - This blocks cross-developer communication and limits access to dev-shared only
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress: allow from namespaces labeled env=dev (the three dev namespaces and dev-shared itself)
  - Egress: allow to namespaces labeled env=dev
- staging and prod:
  - Strictly isolated from dev namespaces
  - Ingress: allow only from same namespace
  - Egress: allow only to same namespace
  - Plus DNS egress as above

Operational notes
- A NetworkPolicy-capable CNI (e.g., Calico, Cilium) must be active for these policies to take effect.
- RBAC is additive. Since we did not grant developers any roles in staging/prod, they cannot access those namespaces unless they already have cluster-wide roles (cluster-admins will continue to have access).
- view in dev-shared does not include reading Secrets by default. If developers must read specific Secrets, I can add a tightly scoped Role to allow get on specific secrets only.

Quick verification tips
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC access checks (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice     → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i delete deploy -n dev-shared --as alice → no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice        → no
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota compute-and-services-quota
- NetworkPolicies: kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy

If you want me to:
- Bind a specific “cluster-admins” group explicitly in staging/prod for clarity
- Allow read of specific Secrets in dev-shared
- Add LimitRanges (default requests/limits per pod/container)
…say the word and I’ll apply those too.

outputSteps.content:
All set. I created the requested namespaces, RBAC, service accounts, resource quotas, and network policies to provide a secure, least-privilege, multi-tenant dev environment for Alice, Bob, and Charlie.

What was created

1) Namespaces
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie
- dev-shared
- staging, prod
- Labels added for policy scoping (e.g., env: dev|staging|prod)

2) RBAC and Service Accounts
- ServiceAccounts:
  - dev-alice/alice-sa
  - dev-bob/bob-sa
  - dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Per-developer full access to own namespace (least-privilege):
  - RoleBinding in each dev namespace binding ClusterRole edit to:
    - the user (alice|bob|charlie)
    - the service account (alice-sa|bob-sa|charlie-sa)
- Read-only access to dev-shared:
  - RoleBinding in dev-shared binding ClusterRole view to:
    - users: alice, bob, charlie
    - service accounts: dev-alice/alice-sa, dev-bob/bob-sa, dev-charlie/charlie-sa
- Staging/prod access:
  - No developer bindings were created in staging or prod (only cluster admins will have access by virtue of their cluster-admin privileges)

Notes on least privilege:
- edit grants full CRUD on namespaced resources but not RBAC; this keeps developers from altering RBAC while letting them manage everything else in their own namespace
- view is read-only and does not include secrets by default (safer for dev-shared). If you need read access to secrets there, tell me and I’ll add a narrowly scoped Role.

3) ResourceQuotas
- dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie:
  - limits.cpu: 2
  - limits.memory: 4Gi
  - requests.cpu: 2
  - requests.memory: 4Gi
  - pods: 10
  - services: 5
- dev-shared:
  - limits.cpu: 4, limits.memory: 8Gi
  - requests.cpu: 4, requests.memory: 8Gi
  - pods: 20, services: 10
- staging, prod:
  - limits.cpu: 8, limits.memory: 16Gi
  - requests.cpu: 8, requests.memory: 16Gi
  - pods: 50, services: 20

4) NetworkPolicies and isolation
- Default deny (Ingress and Egress) in all created namespaces (dev-* / dev-shared / staging / prod)
- DNS/system egress:
  - Allow egress on TCP/UDP 53 to kube-system (CoreDNS) in all created namespaces
- Developer namespaces (dev-alice, dev-bob, dev-charlie):
  - Ingress: allow only from same namespace and from dev-shared
  - Egress: allow only to same namespace and to dev-shared
  - This blocks cross-developer communication and limits access to dev-shared only
- dev-shared:
  - Ingress: allow from namespaces labeled env=dev (the three dev namespaces and dev-shared itself)
  - Egress: allow to namespaces labeled env=dev
- staging and prod:
  - Strictly isolated from dev namespaces
  - Ingress: allow only from same namespace
  - Egress: allow only to same namespace
  - Plus DNS egress as above

Operational notes
- A NetworkPolicy-capable CNI (e.g., Calico, Cilium) must be active for these policies to take effect.
- RBAC is additive. Since we did not grant developers any roles in staging/prod, they cannot access those namespaces unless they already have cluster-wide roles (cluster-admins will continue to have access).
- view in dev-shared does not include reading Secrets by default. If developers must read specific Secrets, I can add a tightly scoped Role to allow get on specific secrets only.

Quick verification tips
- Namespaces: kubectl get ns
- RBAC access checks (example):
  - kubectl auth can-i create deploy -n dev-alice --as alice  → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n dev-shared --as alice     → yes
  - kubectl auth can-i delete deploy -n dev-shared --as alice → no
  - kubectl auth can-i get pods -n staging --as alice        → no
- Quotas: kubectl -n dev-alice describe resourcequota compute-and-services-quota
- NetworkPolicies: kubectl -n dev-alice get networkpolicy

If you want me to:
- Bind a specific “cluster-admins” group explicitly in staging/prod for clarity
- Allow read of specific Secrets in dev-shared
- Add LimitRanges (default requests/limits per pod/container)
…say the word and I’ll apply those too.

results.taskOutput:
Done.

What I set up
- Namespace: statefulset-test
- Headless Service: db (clusterIP: None) for stable network IDs
- StatefulSet: db with 3 replicas
  - Each pod mounts a 1Gi PVC at /data (volumeClaimTemplates: data)
  - initContainer writes the file /data/test with contents: initial_data (only if the file doesn’t already exist)
  - Main container is a simple long-running bash loop to keep the pod alive

Then I scaled the StatefulSet back down to 1 replica. PVCs created for db-1 and db-2 are retained on scale-down.

How to verify
- Pods and scale:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get sts db
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test get pods -l app=db
- Check data in the remaining pod:
  - kubectl -n statefulset-test exec db-0 -- cat /data/test
  - Expected output: initial_data

Notes
- The PVCs for db-0, db-1, and db-2 are each 1Gi and persist even after scaling down, preserving the written data.
